title: Sanjaya tells the Gita
hookLine: a blind king is offered sight to watch the war his sons are fighting, and he says no.
carry: shravana: hearing holy words is devotion
tomorrow: why does Arjuna sit down before the battle?

cards: The armies are drawn up on the field of Kurukshetra. In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits and waits. Then the sage Vyasa comes to him with an offer.
If you want to see the battle, he says, I'll give you sight. And the king says no. He doesn't want to see his own family killed.
He only wants to hear about it. So Vyasa gives the gift to someone else: Sanjaya, the king's charioteer and counselor.
Today the Bhishma book opens, and the Bhagavad Gita, which we've read before, comes back inside the story that holds it.

teach.h: THE GITA PUT BACK IN THE STORY
teach.b: Earlier on the path we read the Gita verse by verse, as a teaching on its own. For these six sessions, we put it back where it lives: in the middle of a war report.

teach.h: THE TELLING STARTS AFTER BHISHMA FALLS
teach.b: After Vyasa's visit, the book doesn't go straight to the first morning of battle.
Instead, Sanjaya comes back to the palace with terrible news. Bhishma, the grandsire of the whole family, has fallen. Days of fighting have already passed.
Dhritarashtra breaks down, and then asks Sanjaya to tell him everything, from the start.

So when the Gita opens with the old king asking what his sons and Pandu's sons did on the field of dharma, he is asking about something already over, the way someone asks after a funeral: tell me how it happened.
Every word Krishna says to Arjuna reaches us through Sanjaya, spoken to a grieving father who refused to look. It's a report in a dark room, to a listener who chose to hear rather than see.
And that's how most Hindus have met the Gita too: by hearing.
The Bhagavata Purana lists nine ways of bhakti, and the first is shravana, hearing holy words and stories.
It's why families play the Gita at home, gather for a katha, and listen at the temple even when the Sanskrit goes past them.

how: The Bhagavad Gita is printed and recited on its own, and it is also read in place as part of the Bhishma Parva, where Sanjaya narrates it to the blind king Dhritarashtra.

s: Dhritarashtra accepted Vyasa's offer to watch the battle
he refused; he didn't want to see his family killed. Sanjaya received the sight instead.
in the epic, the Gita is told after news of Bhishma's fall
Sanjaya returns with the news that Bhishma has fallen, and the king asks him to tell it all from the start.
shravana, hearing, is listed first among bhakti's nine ways
in the Bhagavata Purana's list, hearing holy words comes first.

games.q: you're Dhritarashtra, blind king of the Kurus. a sage offers you sight to watch the war your sons are fighting. what do you say?
o: no: I don't want to see my family killed, but I want to hear it.
no: I want to know nothing.
games.why: he refuses to see, but wants to hear. so Vyasa gives the sight to Sanjaya, and the whole war, Gita included, reaches the king as a report.

practice: Close your eyes and be a listener for a moment, not a watcher. Find the nearest sound, then the farthest one you can hear.
Then, if you pray, listen to one holy word, Om or a name of God, said softly, or one verse of the Gita read aloud. If you don't pray, let the last sound be enough.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma Parva. The Book of Bhishma, the book of the Mahabharata that holds the Bhagavad Gita inside it. This week carried us from the Udyoga embassy, through Karna's two refusals, to this dark room.

orig.note: parva is the Sanskrit word for one of the epic's books; this one is named for Bhishma, the grandsire.

carryVoice: Your line: shravana: hearing holy words is devotion. The Gita you know, told in a dark room. Tomorrow: why does Arjuna sit down before the battle?
